Q: Are semicolons in `for` loops un-pythonic? A:

Yes, using semicolons to concatenate expressions in Python is explicitly discouraged in PEP8 (section Other recommendations; look for "compound statements").

Having maintained Python code bases for much of my career I feel compelled to agree, concatenating statements like this hurts maintainability for no material gain on any other front.

Incidentally, I cannot reproduce your output under CPython 3.13.12. I get reliably alternating 0s and 1s for 20 total lines, meaning that both print statements are considered to be part of the for loop's body; that said, I'm not sure if that parsing is guaranteed by the standard.

I think it's useful to ask in the context, if you were reading this code yourself, how sure are you that that second print is in the for loop's body vs outside of it? Where's the intuition around each of those possibilities?

Q: How do I solve this type hint error "Unexpected type(s)" in PyCharm? A:

The variable redefinition seems to be the main problem. I recommend avoiding the re-assignment in this case, since working around it seems more troublesome than worth it.

From what I've gathered in the comments, the current filename variable (used in the if clause, and on the right side of the assignment to the new variable), is atually more akin to something like filename_suffix (or suffix for short).

Inlining the exerpt you mentioned in your comments, and presuming the type of datum_content_type to be str, we get:

import datetime

from typing import reveal_type

suffix: str | None = None
datum_content_type: str = ''

if suffix: #  i.e. not None
    fn = str(datetime.datetime.now()).replace(":", "-").replace(".", "-") + " - " + datum_content_type + " - " + suffix
    reveal_type(filename) # `str` in inlay hint, corroborated by MyPy.
    with open("files\\" + fn, "wb") as f:
        pass

With no more warnings in the with line :)

Two (tangential) notes:

  1. Please be aware that checking if s: ..., when s is str | None, does not execute the code block if the s is an empty string. This behavior may be desired or not, but be mindful of it. This may trip you up if you come from a C background.

  2. I strongly recommend explicitly choosing how your timestamps are formatted with strftime, instead of relying on the default behavior of datetime.__str__, which is to invoke datetime.isoformat. Luckily (?), in Python, the datetime objects returned by datetime.now are always timezone-naïve, which means consistent string formatting. However, in other languages or scenarios, not explicitly specifying whether to include the timezone in the formatted string can cause a world of hurt later on. This would also have the added benefit of removing the need for the str.replace calls, since you can just set the desired separator(s) in the format template directly :D

Q: Firebase cloud function: How to deal with continuous requests A:

Returning a 403 or empty body on unsupported methods will not do much for you. Yes, you will have less bandwidth wasted, but Firebase will still bill you for the request. The attacker could just send millions of requests and you would still will lose money.

Also, authentication is not a solution to this problem. First of all, any authentication process (create token and verify/validate token) is costly, and again Firebase has thought of this and will bill you based on the time it takes for the function to return a response. You cannot afford to use authentication to prevent continuous requests.

Plus, a smart attacker would not just go for a request which returns 403. What stops the attacker from hitting the login endpoint a millions times?? And if he provides correct credentials (which he would do if he was smart), you will waste bandwidth by returning a token each time, also if you are regenerating tokens you would waste time on each request which would further hurt your bill.

The idea here is to block this attacker completely (before going to your API functions). What I would do is use Cloudflare to proxy my endpoints, and in my API I would define a max_req_limit_per_ip and a time_frame, save each request IP address on the database and on each request check if the IP address did go over the limit for that given time frame. If so, you just use the Cloudflare API to block that IP address at the firewall.

Tip: max_req_limit_per_ip and a time_frame can be custom for different requests.

For example:

  1. an IP address can hit a 403 10 times in one hour
  2. an IP address can hit the login successfully 5 times in 20 minutes
  3. an IP address can hit the login unsuccessfully 5 times in one hour

Q: What is the difference between HTTP 400 and HTTP 422 in REST API validation? A:

1. HTTP 400 Bad Request (syntax / malformed)

Use a 400 status code when the client sends a request that is physically broken or structurally invalid. If the server's JSON parser throws an error before your actual application logic even runs, it's a 400.

When to use it:

  • Malformed JSON: A missing comma, unclosed quote, or trailing bracket ({ "name": "Alice", })
  • Garbage data types: sending a text string where an integer array is strictly required by the protocol
  • Missing mandatory elements: missing a required HTTP header or query parameter that the routing layer depends on

2. HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity (semantics / logic)

Use a 422 status code when the JSON is perfectly valid, but the values inside fail your application's validation or business rules.

When to use it:

  • Field validation failures: a password is too short, an email address is missing a @ character, or a phone number has the wrong number of digits
  • Business logic conflicts: trying to book a hotel room checkout date that is before the check-in date
  • Database duplication: trying to register an account with an email address that is already taken
